newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch brewers face flat markets, seek foreign fizz.
newsitem.headline: Dutch brewers face flat markets, seek foreign fizz.

text.p: Prospects for Dutch brewers look flat due to declining consumption and stiff Europe-wide price competition, but exports to fast-growing markets could provide some fizz, analysts said on Thursday.
The country's third largest brewer Grolsch highlighted the tough market conditions when it announced a meagre 1996 profit rise on Wednesday.
Analysts expect market leader Heinken to unveil 2.5 percent lower annual profits on Friday and keenly await its 1997 outlook.

ING Barings analyst Gerard Rijk said the valuation of the Dutch beer sector had risen sharply since the beginning of the 1990s with its price-earnings ratio outstripping the food sector until last year. "Since last September, they've lost that completely," he said.
The change in sentiment coincided with Heineken's warning that stagnant conditions in key European markets and a poorer summer meant 1996 profits would be lower than the previous year.
Grolsch cited similar factors when it reported a 1.8 percent rise in net profits to 59.9 million guilders for calendar 1996.
Without a six million guilder net gain related to a co-operation agreement, profit would have dipped eight percent.
Grolsch, which ranks behind Heineken and Belgium's privately owned Interbrew in terms of Dutch market share, also forecast lower profits in the current year.
Chairman Paul Snoep said north-west European beer markets had shown signs of saturation since 1990 with beer sales levelling off.
In a sector report issued last month, Dutch financial group Rabobank forecast the western European beer market would dip by 0.3 percent a year until the end of the century.
It said the total European beer market would show an annual growth of 0.4 percent until 2000, with central Europe and the former Soviet Union increasing by an annual 2.5 percent.
The report on world beer markets noted that margins would come under increasing pressure as supermarkets wielded a greater influence over prices.
It said Europe also suffered from a production overcapacity of around 10 percent, mainly in Germany, Britain and Spain.
Official Dutch figures also show a drop in beer consumption in recent years.
Dutch average per capita beer consumption slipped to 83.7 litres in 1996, down 2.4 percent from 85.8 litres in 1995, according to the Dutch central brewing agency.
Rijk said Dutch brewers faced increased competition in saturated markets and added that many, seeing Heineken's success with export beers, were trying to muscle in on foreign markets.
"Marketing costs increase, margins are squeezed," he said.
Grolsh, whose margins were squeezed by intense competition, said it did not see enough room in key markets to raise selling prices in 1997.
Grolsch noted a price war in the German beer market and saw no way to stop the downward trend in the British beer market.
But it said Poland, where it is market leader, was more promising because beer consumption continued to grow.
Rabobank said world beer consumption was set to grow 1.7 percent anually until 2000 to 1.32 billion hectolitres.

Southeast Asia and China were set to show the biggest rise in beer consumption, adding an annual 6.4 percent over the next three years. Asian consumption as a whole was set to increase by 4.5 percent a year. Beer consumption is expected to rise by 2.8 percent a year in South America, it said.
